(b) H. glycines: white lemon-shaped mature females protruding from soybean roots (arrows). Note that soybean cyst nematode does not form root galls. Source: Management of Plant-Parasitic Nematodes in Florida Soybean Production (NG018), UF/IFAS EDIS. Used for educational demonstration only.

Figure 1. A nematode-themed lesson in Lincheng, Hebei. Using images of plant roots, a team member introduces plant-parasitic nematodes and their connection with crop disease, linking familiar plant observations with life below ground and agricultural problems.

Figure 2. Three courses on agricultural nematodes and synthetic biology. (a) The Nematode Hunt introduces nematodes and agricultural problems. (b) Exploring biological signals explains the relationship between input, sensing, and output. (c) Small Lives and Everyday Contributions connects scientific themes with responsibility, cooperation, and personal growth.

Figure 3. Classroom outreach through the Xiangyang Program teaching partnership. Team members and teaching partners bring the materials into classrooms to introduce nematodes and related scientific ideas.

Figure 4. Outreach materials that introduce the project through illustrations and stories. (a) The Yeast Detective and the secret signals in soil. (b) The Yeast Detective’s three steps to helping farmers. Characters, settings, and simple diagrams connect engineered yeast, soil signals, and agricultural applications, giving audiences a visual starting point for understanding the project. Figure 2. Examining receptor localization. GPR2–sfGFP fluorescence is compared with FM4-64 staining and merged images. Scale bars: 10 μm.

Figure 1. Understanding testing needs through field conversations. The team visited growing sites in Tianjin and discussed crop management and disease concerns with local growers. (a) An outdoor conversation; (b) A greenhouse visit.

Figure 2. Public awareness and expectations of a nematode detection tool. (a) Respondents’ awareness of plant-parasitic nematodes; (b) Preferred features of an ideal test. The questionnaire received 369 responses. Respondents could select up to three tool features, with percentages calculated against all 369 responses; percentages in b therefore do not sum to 100%. “Within 15 minutes” describes a proposed testing scenario used to ask about preferences.

Figure 3. Examining the detection concept through expert interviews. Discussions with Yurong Yao addressed agricultural testing needs, signal interpretation, sample conditions, and practical handling.

Figure 4. Geographic origins of samples gathered through our soil collection initiative. Samples from different agricultural and environmental settings connect local conditions with future studies of soil backgrounds, sample preparation, and sensor responses. Markers indicate approximate source areas; samples from tibet are grouped at the regional level.

Figure 5. Materials prepared for corporate outreach. (a) The project presentation; (b), (c) The corporate partnership invitation. The materials brought together agricultural needs, the research concept, potential applications, and requests for support as a basis for discussion.

Figure 6. Explaining agricultural problems and biosensing through classroom teaching. (a) A lesson introducing plant-parasitic nematodes and crop disease; (b) The presentation cover for exploring biological signals, a course connecting biological sensing with the project’s input–response–output concept.

Figure 1. Full-length Gpr2 WT structure predicted locally with AlphaFold 3 [1]. This structure is identified as model_0 in the docking analysis.

Figure 2. Predicted docking poses and pocket environments of Gpr2 WT. (a, b) ascr#3; (c, d) ascr#18. Each pair shows a 3D pocket view and the corresponding Maestro 2D interaction diagram [5] for the lowest-scoring pose. In the 3D views, the receptor is shown as a purple cartoon, pocket residues as yellow sticks, and ascr#3 and ascr#18 in cyan and magenta, respectively. Original residue numbering is retained.
Figure 3. Initial mutation sites in Gpr2. N84, L90, V110, R181, W338, R345, and V368 are highlighted on the predicted full-length structure.

Figure 4. Predicted docking poses and pocket environments of Gpr2 N84V. (a, b) ascr#3; (c, d) ascr#18. Each pair shows a 3D pocket view and the corresponding Maestro 2D interaction diagram for the lowest-scoring pose. Colors follow Figure 2, and residue numbering matches WT.

Figure 5. Predicted docking poses and pocket environments of Gpr2 V368R. (a, b) ascr#3; (c, d) ascr#18. Each pair shows a 3D pocket view and the corresponding Maestro 2D interaction diagram for the lowest-scoring pose. Colors follow Figure 2, and residue numbering matches WT.

Figure 6. Predicted ascaroside-binding pockets in GprC, SRBC-64, and DAF-37. Each receptor shows five docking poses for each of five ascarosides. Cropped from Hu et al. (2024), Figure 5a–c [3], under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license.

Figure 1. Ligand heavy-atom RMSD under three structural alignment schemes. Trajectories were aligned using the whole receptor, the transmembrane helical core, or the local pocket backbone, with each trajectory referenced to its own initial production structure. Curves show a 1 ns centered moving average of data sampled every 100 ps. Shading marks the 50–100 ns comparison window. Each system is represented by one 100 ns trajectory.

Figure 2. Arg189–carboxylate interactions in the Gpr2 N84V–ascr#18 complex. (a) Simulation snapshot at 64.64 ns. The receptor is shown as purple ribbons; ascr#18 and Arg189 are shown as sticks with magenta and yellow carbon atoms, respectively. The dashed line indicates an Arg189–carboxylate hydrogen bond with a donor–acceptor distance of 2.77 Å. (b) Occupancy of at least one Arg189–carboxylate hydrogen bond during 50–100 ns: 93.6% for N84V–ascr#18 and 0% for WT–ascr#18 and N84V–ascr#3. Frames were sampled every 100 ps, using the hydrogen-bond criteria defined in the text.

Figure 3. Changes in ligand anchoring in V368R–ascr#3 simulations initiated from two alternative poses. (a,b) Time-dependent salt-bridge occupancies for the Arg368-directed (a) and Arg189-directed (b) starting poses. Each panel compares the designed Arg368–carboxylate or Arg189–carboxylate contact with the Arg345–carboxylate contact. Shading marks the 50–100 ns comparison window. (c) Arg345–carboxylate contact occupancies during 50–100 ns in the two additional trajectories and the WT–ascr#3, V368R–ascr#18, and original V368R–ascr#3 trajectories. Bars indicate salt-bridge occupancy using a distance cutoff of ≤4 Å; diamonds indicate the occupancy of short, near-linear hydrogen bonds. Each starting pose was simulated for 100 ns.

Figure 1. Sequential calibration workflow for the ODE and dual-channel models.
The upper panel shows mixed-sample design, ODE calibration, and dual-channel regression. The lower panel shows the intended workflow for estimating M. incognita density from paired smartphone readings. Prescribed pigment targets are used to calibrate the ODE, while regression uses color features calculated from the actual ODE outputs. Generated with OpenAI GPT Image 2.

Figure 2. ODE pigment calibration at different background densities.
Panels A and B show P3 and P18, respectively. Colors distinguish C. elegans background densities. Dashed lines with crosses indicate prescribed pigment targets, solid lines with circles indicate simulated 8 h total pigment concentrations, and gray dotted lines indicate the blank.

Figure 3. Net pigment accumulation in representative mixed samples.
Panels A and B show simulated time courses for blank, M. incognita-only, C. elegans-only, and mixed samples in P3 and P18. Net pigment is calculated by subtracting the matched channel blank at each time point.

Figure 4. Distribution of mixed samples in dual-channel color space.
The horizontal and vertical axes show the simulated P3 and P18 smartphone color indices. Point color indicates M. incognita density. Solid lines connect samples with fixed M. incognita density, while dashed lines connect samples with fixed C. elegans density. Arrows indicate the directions of increasing M. incognita or C. elegans density.

Figure 5. M. incognita density predictions and comparison of single- and dual-channel models.
Panel A compares known and predicted M. incognita densities for the dual-channel model; the dashed line indicates ideal agreement. Panel B compares the RMSEs of P3-only, P18-only, and dual-channel models on the same simulated evaluation set.
